claim: Drosophila neural progenitors (neuroblasts) have been an excellent model for studying self-renewal and differentiation.
source: Drosophila neural progenitors (neuroblasts) have been an excellent model for studying self-renewal and differentiation, but quiescence remains poorly understood.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field, representing consensus about the utility of the Drosophila neuroblast model system.

claim: Quiescence in Drosophila neuroblasts remains poorly understood.
source: Drosophila neural progenitors (neuroblasts) have been an excellent model for studying self-renewal and differentiation, but quiescence remains poorly understood.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the field, representing the current state of understanding.

claim: When neuroblasts enter quiescence, the differentiation factor Prospero is transiently detected in the neuroblast nucleus.
source: In this study, we show that when neuroblasts enter quiescence, the differentiation factor Prospero is transiently detected in the neuroblast nucleus, followed by the establishment of a unique molecular profile lacking most progenitor and differentiation markers.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 2.

claim: Quiescent neuroblasts establish a unique molecular profile lacking most progenitor and differentiation markers.
source: In this study, we show that when neuroblasts enter quiescence, the differentiation factor Prospero is transiently detected in the neuroblast nucleus, followed by the establishment of a unique molecular profile lacking most progenitor and differentiation markers.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The pulse of low level nuclear Prospero precedes entry into neuroblast quiescence even when the timing of quiescence is advanced or delayed by changing temporal identity factors.
source: The pulse of low level nuclear Prospero precedes entry into neuroblast quiescence even when the timing of quiescence is advanced or delayed by changing temporal identity factors.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 2E,F showing correlation between Prospero timing and quiescence timing in pdm and cas mutants.

claim: Loss of Prospero prevents entry into quiescence.
source: Furthermore, loss of Prospero prevents entry into quiescence, whereas a pulse of low level nuclear Prospero can drive proliferating larval neuroblasts into quiescence.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 3 showing prospero mutants fail to enter quiescence.

claim: A pulse of low level nuclear Prospero can drive proliferating larval neuroblasts into quiescence.
source: Furthermore, loss of Prospero prevents entry into quiescence, whereas a pulse of low level nuclear Prospero can drive proliferating larval neuroblasts into quiescence.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 4 showing transient Prospero expression induces quiescence.

claim: Prospero levels distinguish three progenitor fates: absent for self-renewal, low for quiescence, and high for differentiation.
source: We propose that Prospero levels distinguish three progenitor fates: absent for self-renewal, low for quiescence, and high for differentiation.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the experimental findings throughout the study, representing an inference from the data.

claim: Quiescent stem cells preserve the stem cell pool for activation following disease or injury.
source: Quiescent stem cells preserve the stem cell pool for activation following disease or injury.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about stem cell biology.

claim: Cancer stem cells can enter remission during treatment, possibly using mechanisms similar to stem cell quiescence, and re-initiate proliferation months to years later.
source: Moreover, cancer stem cells can enter remission during treatment, possibly using mechanisms similar to stem cell quiescence, and re-initiate proliferation months to years later.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about cancer stem cell behavior, with speculation about the mechanism.

claim: Studying stem cell quiescence may help design clinical approaches to prevent tumor dormancy and cancer recurrence.
source: Thus, studying stem cell quiescence may help design clinical approaches to prevent tumor dormancy and cancer recurrence, as well as to aid in activating stem cells for tissue repair.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential clinical applications.

claim: Studying stem cell quiescence may aid in activating stem cells for tissue repair.
source: Thus, studying stem cell quiescence may help design clinical approaches to prevent tumor dormancy and cancer recurrence, as well as to aid in activating stem cells for tissue repair.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential clinical applications.

claim: Drosophila neuroblasts have served as a model system for identifying conserved signaling pathways that regulate stem cell proliferation and quiescence.
source: Drosophila neuroblasts have served as a model system for identifying conserved signaling pathways that regulate stem cell proliferation and quiescence (Ebens et al., 1993; Datta, 1995; Britton and Edgar, 1998; Doe et al., 1998; Egger et al., 2008; Tsuji et al., 2008; Sousa-Nunes et al., 2010; Homem and Knoblich, 2012; Weng and Cohen, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work in the field.

claim: Drosophila neuroblasts delaminate from neuroectoderm during early embryogenesis.
source: Drosophila neuroblasts delaminate from neuroectoderm during early embryogenesis, and then they go through multiple rounds of asymmetric cell division before exiting cell cycle at the end of embryogenesis
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about Drosophila neuroblast development.

claim: Drosophila neuroblasts go through multiple rounds of asymmetric cell division before exiting cell cycle at the end of embryogenesis.
source: Drosophila neuroblasts delaminate from neuroectoderm during early embryogenesis, and then they go through multiple rounds of asymmetric cell division before exiting cell cycle at the end of embryogenesis
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about Drosophila neuroblast development.

claim: Upon cell cycle exit, neuroblasts can undergo apoptosis.
source: upon cell cycle exit, neuroblasts can undergo apoptosis (Karcavitch and Doe, 2005; Maurange and Gould, 2005; Ulvklo et al., 2012) or enter quiescence (Truman and Bate, 1988; Datta, 1995; Tsuji et al., 2008; Chell and Brand, 2010; Sousa-Nunes et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Upon cell cycle exit, neuroblasts can enter quiescence.
source: upon cell cycle exit, neuroblasts can undergo apoptosis (Karcavitch and Doe, 2005; Maurange and Gould, 2005; Ulvklo et al., 2012) or enter quiescence (Truman and Bate, 1988; Datta, 1995; Tsuji et al., 2008; Chell and Brand, 2010; Sousa-Nunes et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: During neuroblast asymmetric division, the scaffolding protein Miranda (Mira) is partitioned into the differentiating daughter cell, called a ganglion mother cell (GMC).
source: During neuroblast asymmetric division, the scaffolding protein Miranda (Mira) is partitioned into the differentiating daughter cell, called a ganglion mother cell (GMC), and it carries at least three cargo proteins: the translational repressors Staufen and Brain tumor (Brat) and the transcriptional repressor Prospero (Hirata et al., 1995; Broadus and Doe, 1997; Ikeshima-Kataoka et al., 1997; Broadus et al., 1998; Schuldt et al., 1998; Shen et al., 1998; Bello et al., 2006; Betschinger et al., 2006; Lee et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Miranda carries at least three cargo proteins: the translational repressors Staufen and Brain tumor (Brat) and the transcriptional repressor Prospero.
source: During neuroblast asymmetric division, the scaffolding protein Miranda (Mira) is partitioned into the differentiating daughter cell, called a ganglion mother cell (GMC), and it carries at least three cargo proteins: the translational repressors Staufen and Brain tumor (Brat) and the transcriptional repressor Prospero (Hirata et al., 1995; Broadus and Doe, 1997; Ikeshima-Kataoka et al., 1997; Broadus et al., 1998; Schuldt et al., 1998; Shen et al., 1998; Bello et al., 2006; Betschinger et al., 2006; Lee et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In the GMC, Mira appears to be degraded and its cargo is released into the cytoplasm (Staufen, Brat) or the nucleus (Prospero).
source: In the GMC, Mira appears to be degraded and its cargo is released into the cytoplasm (Staufen, Brat) or the nucleus (Prospero).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about Miranda function in GMCs.

claim: Prospero is an atypical homeodomain protein that directly binds and represses progenitor and cell cycle genes to initiate GMC and neuronal differentiation.
source: Prospero is an atypical homeodomain protein that directly binds and represses progenitor and cell cycle genes to initiate GMC and neuronal differentiation (Li and Vaessin, 2000; Choksi et al., 2006)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The mammalian ortholog Prox1 has a similar role in repressing cell cycle gene expression.
source: the mammalian ortholog Prox1 has a similar role in repressing cell cycle gene expression (Dyer, 2003; Foskolou et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Keeping high levels of Prospero out of the neuroblast nucleus is essential to prevent neuroblast differentiation.
source: In addition, keeping high levels of Prospero out of the neuroblast nucleus is essential to prevent neuroblast differentiation (Choksi et al., 2006; Cabernard and Doe, 2009; Bayraktar et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Low levels of Prospero repress all cell cycle and progenitor genes except deadpan.
source: We propose a model in which low levels of Prospero repress all cell cycle and progenitor genes except deadpan, whereas high levels of Prospero additionally repress deadpan to allow neural differentiation.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental findings, representing an inference from the data.

claim: High levels of Prospero additionally repress deadpan to allow neural differentiation.
source: We propose a model in which low levels of Prospero repress all cell cycle and progenitor genes except deadpan, whereas high levels of Prospero additionally repress deadpan to allow neural differentiation.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental findings, representing an inference from the data.

claim: Neuroblast 3-3 in the thoracic segments (NB3-3T) reliably enters quiescence at embryonic stage 15.
source: As a model system we used the identified neuroblast 3–3 in the thoracic segments (NB3-3T) which reliably enters quiescence at embryonic stage 15 (Tsuji et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Neuroblast 3-3 in abdominal segments (NB3-3A) remains proliferative until the end of embryogenesis.
source: Moreover, neuroblast 3–3 in abdominal segments (NB3-3A) remains proliferative until the end of embryogenesis and provides an excellent internal control (Tsuji et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The quiescent NB3-3T can be recognized by Deadpan, a basic helix-loop-helix transcription factor.
source: Previous work showed that the quiescent NB3-3T can be recognized by Deadpan, a basic helix-loop-helix transcription factor (Zhu et al., 2008; Chell and Brand, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The coiled-coil Miranda protein marks quiescent neuroblasts.
source: The coiled-coil Miranda protein is also reported to mark quiescent neuroblasts (Tsuji et al., 2008), which we confirm here (Figure 1)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work and confirmed by data in Figure 1.

claim: mira transcription is down-regulated in quiescent neuroblasts based on lack of mRNA in the stage 17 CNS in the BDGP in situ database.
source: but note that mira transcription is down-regulated in quiescent neuroblasts based lack of mRNA in the stage 17 CNS in the BDGP in situ database (Tomancak et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a database resource.

claim: All tested progenitor markers—Worniu, Asense, and Cyclin E (CycE)—are not expressed in the quiescent NB3-3T.
source: Interestingly, we find that all other tested progenitor markers—Worniu, Asense, and Cyclin E (CycE) (Brand et al., 1993; Caldwell and Datta, 1998; Ashraf et al., 2004; Lai et al., 2012)—are not expressed in the quiescent NB3-3T (Figure 1; data not shown)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Progenitor markers Worniu, Asense, and CycE can be robustly detected in the proliferative NB3-3A.
source: although they can be robustly detected in the proliferative NB3-3A (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Larval quiescent neuroblasts lack expression of Worniu, Asense, CycE (and Miranda), while retaining Deadpan protein and active deadpan transcription.
source: Similarly, larval quiescent neuroblasts lack expression of Worniu, Asense, CycE (and Miranda), while retaining Deadpan protein and active deadpan transcription (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Misexpression of Worniu, Asense, or CycE has no effect on the timing of NB3-3T quiescence.
source: However, misexpression of Worniu (data not shown), Asense, or CycE (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) has no effect on the timing of NB3-3T quiescence.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The mature quiescent NB3-3T did not express nuclear Prospero, Elav, or Repo.
source: We found that the mature quiescent NB3-3T did not express nuclear Prospero, Elav, or Repo (data not shown)
evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation.

claim: Differentiation markers nuclear Prospero, Elav, and Repo were not observed in quiescent larval brain neuroblasts.
source: nor were these differentiation markers observed in quiescent larval brain neuroblasts (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: NB3-3T showed a pulse of nuclear Prospero at stage 15 concurrent with entry into quiescence.
source: Whereas NB3-3T showed a pulse of nuclear Prospero at stage 15 concurrent with entry into quiescence (Figure 2A,B)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: NB3-3A did not show nuclear Prospero and did not enter quiescence.
source: NB3-3A did not show nuclear Prospero and did not enter quiescence (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C,D.

claim: The levels of Prospero in the NB3-3T neuroblast are clearly detectable by immunofluorescent staining, but at significantly lower levels than in differentiating GMCs.
source: The levels of Prospero in the NB3-3T neuroblast are clearly detectable by immunofluorescent staining, but at significantly lower levels than in differentiating GMCs (Figure 2B, arrow; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: nubbin/pdm2 (pdm) mutants cause precocious NB3-3T quiescence.
source: nubbin/pdm2 (pdm) mutants cause precocious NB3-3T quiescence, whereas castor (cas) mutants cause a delay in NB3-3T quiescence (Tsuji et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: castor (cas) mutants cause a delay in NB3-3T quiescence.
source: nubbin/pdm2 (pdm) mutants cause precocious NB3-3T quiescence, whereas castor (cas) mutants cause a delay in NB3-3T quiescence (Tsuji et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The pulse of nuclear Prospero precisely matched the timing of neuroblast quiescence: it occurred earlier in pdm mutants, and later in cas mutants.
source: Strikingly, the pulse of nuclear Prospero precisely matched the timing of neuroblast quiescence: it occurred earlier in pdm mutants, and later in cas mutants (Figure 2E,F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E,F.

claim: prospero mutants show de-differentiation of GMCs into proliferating neuroblasts.
source: The problem is that prospero mutants show de-differentiation of GMCs into proliferating neuroblasts (Choksi et al., 2006; Lee et al., 2006)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: During neuroblast asymmetric cell division, Miranda-Prospero and Partner of numb (Pon)-Numb protein complexes are independently segregated into the GMC to promote differentiation.
source: During neuroblast asymmetric cell division, Miranda-Prospero and Partner of numb (Pon)-Numb protein complexes are independently segregated into the GMC to promote differentiation (Doe, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: In prospero mutants, Numb is still properly segregated to GMCs where it represses Notch activity.
source: In prospero mutants, Numb is still properly segregated to GMCs where it represses Notch activity (Spana and Doe, 1995)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: In prospero mutants, the Notch reporter mγ-LacZ is restricted to parental neuroblasts.
source: and consequently the Notch reporter mγ-LacZ is restricted to parental neuroblasts.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known function of Numb in repressing Notch activity.

claim: mγ-LacZ is transcribed only in neuroblasts.
source: mγ-LacZ is transcribed only in neuroblasts; in wild type the protein perdures into neuroblast progeny, whereas in prospero mutants the protein is restricted to neuroblasts because the progeny proliferate without expressing mγ-LacZ and thus dilute out the protein (Choksi et al., 2006; Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work and data in Figure 3A,B.

claim: In wild type, mγ-LacZ protein perdures into neuroblast progeny.
source: mγ-LacZ is transcribed only in neuroblasts; in wild type the protein perdures into neuroblast progeny, whereas in prospero mutants the protein is restricted to neuroblasts because the progeny proliferate without expressing mγ-LacZ and thus dilute out the protein (Choksi et al., 2006; Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work and data in Figure 3A,B.

claim: In prospero mutants, mγ-LacZ protein is restricted to neuroblasts because the progeny proliferate without expressing mγ-LacZ and thus dilute out the protein.
source: mγ-LacZ is transcribed only in neuroblasts; in wild type the protein perdures into neuroblast progeny, whereas in prospero mutants the protein is restricted to neuroblasts because the progeny proliferate without expressing mγ-LacZ and thus dilute out the protein (Choksi et al., 2006; Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work and data in Figure 3A,B.

claim: In wild type, nearly all neuroblasts ceased EdU incorporation by stage 16.
source: Whereas in wild type nearly all neuroblasts ceased EdU incorporation by stage 16 (Figure 3A)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Many mγ-LacZ+ neuroblasts continued to incorporate EdU in prospero mutants at stage 16.
source: many mγ-LacZ+ neuroblasts continued to incorporate EdU in prospero mutants at the same stage (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Prospero is unique among basal cell fate determinants in regulating neuroblast quiescence.
source: In addition, Prospero is unique among basal cell fate determinants in regulating neuroblast quiescence: loss of function mutations in numb or brat, or the Prospero target gene string, showed no effect on the timing of neuroblast quiescence (data not shown).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations (data not shown).

claim: Loss of function mutations in numb or brat, or the Prospero target gene string, showed no effect on the timing of neuroblast quiescence.
source: In addition, Prospero is unique among basal cell fate determinants in regulating neuroblast quiescence: loss of function mutations in numb or brat, or the Prospero target gene string, showed no effect on the timing of neuroblast quiescence (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation.

claim: In both wild type and prospero haplo-insufficiency embryos, the mγ-LacZ+ NB3-3T was proliferative at stage 14 and quiescent by stage 16.
source: In both wild type and prospero haplo-insufficiency embryos, the mγ-LacZ+ NB3-3T was proliferative at stage 14 and quiescent by stage 16 (Figure 3C, quantified in Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and 3E.

claim: In prospero mutant embryos, the mγ-LacZ+ NB3-3T was proliferative at both stage 14 and 16.
source: In prospero mutant embryos, the mγ-LacZ+ NB3-3T was proliferative at both stage 14 and 16 (Figure 3D, quantified in Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D and 3E.

claim: The level of Prospero required for neuroblast quiescence is lower than that in prospero haplo-insufficiency.
source: The results suggest that the level of Prospero required for neuroblast quiescence is lower than that in prospero haplo-insufficiency and that a low level of Prospero is sufficient to promote neuroblast quiescence (see next section).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results showing that haplo-insufficiency does not affect quiescence timing.

claim: A low level of Prospero is sufficient to promote neuroblast quiescence.
source: The results suggest that the level of Prospero required for neuroblast quiescence is lower than that in prospero haplo-insufficiency and that a low level of Prospero is sufficient to promote neuroblast quiescence (see next section).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results and is further supported by data in the next section.

claim: The central brain neuroblasts are continuously proliferating during the third larval instar.
source: The central brain neuroblasts are continuously proliferating during the third larval instar (Ito and Hotta, 1992)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: High levels of Prospero can induce neuroblast differentiation.
source: Because high levels of Prospero can induce neuroblast differentiation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) (Choksi et al., 2006; Cabernard and Doe, 2009; Bayraktar et al., 2010)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work and data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: In wild-type larval brains, there are few or no quiescent neuroblasts.
source: In wild-type larval brains, we found few or no quiescent neuroblasts, as expected (Figure 4E,F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E,F.

claim: A pulse of Prospero resulted in the appearance of numerous quiescent neuroblasts.
source: In contrast, a pulse of Prospero resulted in the appearance of numerous quiescent neuroblasts (Figure 4E,F; 12 hr timepoint).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E,F.

claim: Nearly all of the neuroblasts that were quiescent at 12 hr after Prospero induction had reactivated proliferation and re-expressed progenitor markers at 24 hr.
source: We found that nearly all of the neuroblasts that were quiescent at 12 hr after induction had reactivated proliferation and re-expressed progenitor markers (Figure 4E,F; 24 hr timepoint).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E,F.

claim: Precocious low level nuclear Prospero could advance the timing of NB3-3T quiescence.
source: In addition, precocious low level nuclear Prospero could advance the timing of NB3-3T quiescence (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Prospero can transiently arrest the cell cycle without inducing differentiation in embryonic longitudinal glial progenitors.
source: Interestingly, Prospero can also transiently arrest the cell cycle without inducing differentiation in embryonic longitudinal glial progenitors (Griffiths and Hidalgo, 2004), although the relative levels of Prospero have not been explored in this system.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: High levels of the vertebrate ortholog Prox1 can trigger differentiation.
source: Our results confirm that high levels of Prospero can trigger differentiation and reveal that low levels of Prospero induce quiescence in the Drosophila neuroblasts. High levels of the vertebrate ortholog Prox1 can also trigger differentiation (Dyer, 2003; Takahashi et al., 2006; Foskolou et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Low levels of nuclear Prospero promote neuroblast quiescence without triggering differentiation.
source: thus it is interesting that low levels of nuclear Prospero promote neuroblast quiescence without triggering differentiation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Prox1 activates some target genes at high levels but represses some target genes at low levels.
source: Prox1 activates some target genes at high levels but represses some target genes at low levels (Chen et al., 2008a, 2008b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Low levels of Prospero are sufficient to repress most progenitor-specific genes in neuroblasts (worniu, asense, miranda, and cycE) but do not repress the expression of deadpan.
source: We suggest a speculative model for Prospero function: low levels of Prospero are sufficient to repress most progenitor-specific genes in neuroblasts (worniu, asense, miranda, and cycE) but do not repress the expression of deadpan (perhaps due to lack of high affinity Prospero binding sites).
evidence: This is a speculative model proposed based on the experimental findings.

claim: High levels of Prospero are sufficient to repress deadpan and may even activate neuronal differentiation genes.
source: In contrast, high levels of Prospero are sufficient to repress deadpan (perhaps via low affinity binding sites) and may even activate neuronal differentiation genes (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is a speculative model proposed based on the experimental findings.

claim: In embryonic neuroblasts, the temporal transcription factors Pdm and Cas schedule the timing of neuroblast quiescence.
source: In embryonic neuroblasts, the temporal transcription factors Pdm and Cas schedule the timing of neuroblast quiescence, but how they regulate Prospero nuclear import is unknown.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with an acknowledgment of an unknown mechanism.

claim: How temporal transcription factors Pdm and Cas regulate Prospero nuclear import is unknown.
source: In embryonic neuroblasts, the temporal transcription factors Pdm and Cas schedule the timing of neuroblast quiescence, but how they regulate Prospero nuclear import is unknown.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap.

claim: In larval neuroblasts, Grh prevents accumulation of nuclear Prospero which would induce neuroblast cell cycle exit and differentiation.
source: In larval neuroblasts, Grh prevents accumulation of nuclear Prospero which would induce neuroblast cell cycle exit and differentiation (Maurange et al., 2008; Chai et al., 2013), again by an unknown mechanism.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The mechanism by which Grh prevents accumulation of nuclear Prospero is unknown.
source: In larval neuroblasts, Grh prevents accumulation of nuclear Prospero which would induce neuroblast cell cycle exit and differentiation (Maurange et al., 2008; Chai et al., 2013), again by an unknown mechanism.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap.

claim: The protein Caliban is known to promote Prospero nuclear export in S2 cells.
source: The protein Caliban is known to promote Prospero nuclear export in S2 cells (Bi et al., 2005)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: It is unknown whether Caliban has a similar role in neuroblasts or if down-regulation of Caliban levels or activity leads to increased nuclear Prospero in neuroblasts entering quiescence.
source: but it is unknown whether Caliban has a similar role in neuroblasts or if down-regulation of Caliban levels or activity leads to increased nuclear Prospero in neuroblasts entering quiescence.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap and speculation about a possible mechanism.

claim: Proliferating NB3-3A contains cytoplasmic Mira at embryonic stages 14 and 16.
source: (A–F) Proliferating NB3-3A contains nuclear Deadpan (A), cytoplasmic Mira (B), nuclear Asense (C), nuclear Worniu (D), and nuclear CycE (E) at embryonic stages 14 and 16; quantification is shown in (F).

claim: Proliferating NB3-3A contains nuclear Asense at embryonic stages 14 and 16.
source: (A–F) Proliferating NB3-3A contains nuclear Deadpan (A), cytoplasmic Mira (B), nuclear Asense (C), nuclear Worniu (D), and nuclear CycE (E) at embryonic stages 14 and 16; quantification is shown in (F).

claim: Proliferating NB3-3A contains nuclear Worniu at embryonic stages 14 and 16.
source: (A–F) Proliferating NB3-3A contains nuclear Deadpan (A), cytoplasmic Mira (B), nuclear Asense (C), nuclear Worniu (D), and nuclear CycE (E) at embryonic stages 14 and 16; quantification is shown in (F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Proliferating NB3-3A contains nuclear CycE at embryonic stages 14 and 16.
source: (A–F) Proliferating NB3-3A contains nuclear Deadpan (A), cytoplasmic Mira (B), nuclear Asense (C), nuclear Worniu (D), and nuclear CycE (E) at embryonic stages 14 and 16; quantification is shown in (F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Proliferating NB3-3T expresses all neuroblast markers (Deadpan, Mira, Asense, Worniu, CycE) at stage 14.
source: (G–L) Proliferating NB3-3T expresses all above-mentioned neuroblast markers at stage 14 (S14).

claim: The newly hatched larval (NHL) central brain contains five persistently proliferative neuroblasts.
source: (A) The newly hatched larval (NHL) central brain contains five persistently proliferative neuroblasts (the four mushroom body neuroblasts and the lateral antennal lobe neuroblast) and ∼100 quiescent central brain neuroblasts in each lobe.

source: (A) The newly hatched larval (NHL) central brain contains five persistently proliferative neuroblasts (the four mushroom body neuroblasts and the lateral antennal lobe neuroblast) and ∼100 quiescent central brain neuroblasts in each lobe.

claim: Proliferative neuroblasts in the newly hatched larval brain contain progenitor markers Deadpan, Asense, and Worniu.

claim: Proliferative neuroblasts in the newly hatched larval brain lack the differentiation markers Prospero, Elav, and Repo.

source: (B–E) Proliferative neuroblasts in the NHL contain progenitor markers Deadpan (Dpn), Asense (Ase), and Worniu (Wor) but lack the differentiation markers Prospero (Pros), Elav, and Repo and incorporate EdU (top).

claim: Quiescent neuroblasts in the newly hatched larval brain maintain Deadpan but lack the progenitor markers and the differentiation markers, and fail to incorporate EdU.
source: Quiescent neuroblasts maintain Dpn, but lack the progenitor markers and the differentiation markers, and fail to incorporate EdU (bottom).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B-E.

claim: Transient overexpression of nuclear Prospero in neuroblasts results in neuroblast quiescence or differentiation.
source: (A–C) Transient overexpression of nuclear Prospero in neuroblasts (worniu-gal4 UAS-HA:prospero tub-gal80ts) results in neuroblast quiescence (A) or differentiation (B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4A-C.

claim: Low levels of nuclear Prospero result in neuroblast quiescence (Dpn+ Elav−).
source: Low levels of nuclear Prospero result in neuroblast quiescence (Dpn+ Elav−) (A) whereas high levels of nuclear Prospero suppress Deadpan and activate Elav to induce differentiation (Dpn− Elav+) (B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: High levels of nuclear Prospero suppress Deadpan and activate Elav to induce differentiation (Dpn− Elav+).
source: Low levels of nuclear Prospero result in neuroblast quiescence (Dpn+ Elav−) (A) whereas high levels of nuclear Prospero suppress Deadpan and activate Elav to induce differentiation (Dpn− Elav+) (B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Differentiated neuroblasts have higher Prospero intensity than quiescent neuroblasts.
source: (C) Quantification of Prospero levels in quiescent neuroblasts (Dpn+ Elav−) or differentiated neuroblasts (Dpn− Elav+).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Upon transient overexpression of Prospero, neuroblasts stay Deadpan+ and thus do not differentiate.
source: (D) Neuroblasts stay Deadpan+ (Dpn+) and thus do not differentiate.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: There is an increase of quiescent neuroblasts 12 hr after Prospero induction, as determined by the elevated percentage of EdU− and Wor− neuroblasts.
source: (E) There is an increase of quiescent neuroblasts 12 hr after Prospero induction, as determined by the elevated percentage of EdU− (D) and Wor− (E) neuroblasts.

claim: The quiescent neuroblasts re-enter the cell cycle and express the progenitor marker Wor 24 hr after Prospero induction.
source: The quiescent neuroblasts re-enter the cell cycle and express the progenitor marker Wor 24 hr after induction.
